```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%",
                      dpi = 150)
library(hypergraphs)
has_igraph <- requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
comma <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
```

Legal datasets contain relations involving several entities within a
single observation. An arbitral tribunal groups its arbitrators within a
case. A citation block groups earlier decisions cited together in one
passage of a judgment. A hypergraph represents these observed groups as
hyperedges, retaining membership that a pairwise network cannot recover
from its edges alone.

This tutorial reconstructs selected analyses of Coupette, Hartung, and
Katz (2024) from their released data. It introduces temporal construction,
snapshots, alternative representations, growth measures, null models,
hyperedge centrality, motifs, and community detection. An additional
analysis examines hypergraph modularity. Some simulation and optimisation
settings are reduced for the tutorial and are stated explicitly, so the
results are not presented as an exact replication of every published
estimate.

## Data

The package includes data released by Coupette, Hartung, and Katz
(2024), with source and licence information recorded in the dataset help
pages. The release is archived as Zenodo record 8081507 under CC BY-NC 4.0.
`icsid_tribunals` contains one row per seat on an International Centre for
Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) tribunal. Rows identify the case,
seat, arbitrator, constitution date, conclusion date, and case attributes
such as economic sector. A missing conclusion date indicates an open
observation interval in this analysis.

```{r data-icsid}
head(icsid_tribunals)
```

```{r data-icsid-values, include = FALSE}
n_cases <- length(unique(icsid_tribunals$case))
n_arbitrators <- length(unique(icsid_tribunals$arbitrator))
n_pending <- length(unique(subset(icsid_tribunals, !is_concluded)$case))
```

The dataset contains `r comma(n_cases)` cases and
`r comma(n_arbitrators)` arbitrators. At the observation endpoint of
15 June 2023, `r n_pending` cases were recorded as pending.

The German Federal Constitutional Court (GFCC) data use two tables.
`gfcc_decisions` contains decision identifiers and dates.
`gfcc_citations` records individual citations, their citing and cited
decisions, their citation blocks, and the corresponding dates. Keeping
decision metadata separate permits the node universe to include decisions
that are never cited.

```{r data-gfcc}
head(gfcc_citations)
```

```{r data-gfcc-values, include = FALSE}
n_decisions <- nrow(gfcc_decisions)
n_citations <- nrow(gfcc_citations)
n_blocks <- length(unique(gfcc_citations$block))
first_year <- format(min(gfcc_decisions$date), "%Y")
last_year <- format(max(gfcc_decisions$date), "%Y")
```

The release contains `r comma(n_decisions)` decisions dated between
`r first_year` and `r last_year`, with `r comma(n_citations)` citations
grouped into `r comma(n_blocks)` blocks.

## Temporal hypergraphs

Temporal construction begins with a membership table and declared
clock columns. For interval data, `start` and `end` define when a
membership is active. For contact data, `time` identifies an instantaneous
event. Tribunal case intervals use the first format; citation blocks dated
by the citing decision use the second. Calendar dates are stored relative
to a reported origin and unit. The underlying date conversion does not
change the interpretation of the observation interval.

For tribunals, specify the arbitrator column as `node`, the case
column as `hyperedge`, and the constitution and conclusion dates as
`start` and `end`. An open interval remains active through the declared
`observation_end`. A column constant within a case, such as economic
sector, is retained as a hyperedge attribute. Activity here refers to the
recorded case interval, not continuous joint work by the arbitrators.

```{r icsid-build}
tribunals <- temporal_hypergraph(icsid_tribunals, node = "arbitrator",
                                 hyperedge = "case", start = "constituted",
                                 end = "concluded",
                                 observation_end = as.Date("2023-06-15"))
summary(tribunals)
```

Each tribunal contains three arbitrators. The mean observed interval
is `r comma(round(summary(tribunals)$mean_duration))` days. Open cases are
bounded by the observation endpoint, so this summary is not an estimate
of mean completed-case duration.

For citation blocks, cited decisions are nodes, blocks are hyperedges,
and the citing decision's date is the contact time. Supply the decision
table through `nodes` to include every decision from its own entry date,
including uncited decisions. The citing-decision identifier is constant
within a block and becomes a hyperedge attribute. `sparse = TRUE` stores
the incidence without allocating a cell for every absent membership.

```{r gfcc-build}
blocks <- temporal_hypergraph(gfcc_citations, node = "cited",
                              hyperedge = "block", time = "date_citing",
                              nodes = gfcc_decisions, sparse = TRUE)
summary(blocks)
```

```{r gfcc-build-values, include = FALSE}
block_summary <- summary(blocks)
```

The median block size is `r block_summary$median_edge_size` cited
decisions, and the mean is
`r sprintf("%.2f", block_summary$mean_edge_size)`. These quantities
correspond to the citation-block summaries in Table 1 of Coupette et al.
(2024).

## Snapshots and representations

A snapshot selects the memberships present under a specified temporal
rule. At a single time, `mode = "active"` selects intervals containing
that time and contacts occurring at that instant. `mode = "cumulative"`
selects everything observed up to that time. The cumulative snapshot at
the observation endpoint is the aggregate hypergraph.
`multiedges = FALSE` combines hyperedges with identical member sets.

```{r snapshots}
tribunals_all <- hg_snapshot(tribunals, mode = "cumulative")
tribunals_active <- hg_snapshot(tribunals, at = as.Date("2023-06-15"),
                                mode = "active", multiedges = FALSE)
blocks_all <- hg_snapshot(blocks, mode = "cumulative")
```

Compare four representations of the same observations. The
multi-hypergraph (`mh`) retains every observed group, while the binary
hypergraph (`bh`) retains each distinct member set once. Their graph
projections either count repeated pairwise edges (`mg`) or merge them
(`bg`). In the tribunal clique projection, an edge joins two arbitrators
who share a tribunal. Binary graph degree counts distinct colleagues;
hyperdegree counts incident tribunals. These measures have different
observational units.

```{r icsid-representations}
hg_representations(tribunals_all)
```

```{r icsid-representations-values, include = FALSE}
icsid_reps <- hg_representations(tribunals_all)
icsid_rep <- function(r, col) unlist(subset(icsid_reps, representation == r, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

The median number of distinct colleagues is
`r icsid_rep("bg", "median_degree")`, while the median number of tribunals
is `r icsid_rep("mh", "median_degree")`. The
`r comma(icsid_rep("mh", "n_edges"))` tribunals contain
`r comma(icsid_rep("bh", "n_edges"))` distinct panels. Thus,
`r icsid_rep("mh", "n_edges") - icsid_rep("bh", "n_edges")`
observations repeat a member set already counted. This is a count of
repetition, without an assumption about how the panels were selected.

For the GFCC data, use the source-to-member citation graph. Each
citing decision is connected to the decisions cited in its blocks.
`graph = "citation"` selects this projection, and `edge_source` identifies
the hyperedge attribute containing the citing decision.

```{r gfcc-representations}
hg_representations(blocks_all, graph = "citation", edge_source = "citing")
```

```{r gfcc-representations-values, include = FALSE}
gfcc_reps <- hg_representations(blocks_all, graph = "citation",
                                 edge_source = "citing")
gfcc_rep <- function(r, col) unlist(subset(gfcc_reps, representation == r, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

The median binary out-degree is
`r gfcc_rep("bg", "median_out_degree")` cited decisions. The median
hyperdegree is `r gfcc_rep("mh", "median_degree")` citation-block
memberships. There are `r comma(gfcc_rep("mh", "n_edges"))` blocks and
`r comma(gfcc_rep("bh", "n_edges"))` distinct cited-decision sets,
giving `r sprintf("%.1f", gfcc_rep("mh", "n_edges") / gfcc_rep("bh", "n_edges"))`
blocks per distinct set on average. These are representation summaries
corresponding to Table 2 of Coupette et al. (2024).

## One decision as a hypergraph

```{r headscarf-date, include = FALSE}
headscarf_date <- subset(gfcc_decisions, decision == "153-001")$date
```

A single judgment can be examined as a hypergraph of its citation
blocks. The following subset selects blocks whose `citing` attribute is
decision 153-001, dated `r format(headscarf_date, "%e %B %Y")`
(Kopftuch III). The operation selects recorded citation structure and
does not evaluate the legal significance of the cited decisions.

```{r headscarf}
headscarf <- hg_subset(blocks_all, where = c(citing = "153-001"))
headscarf
```

```{r headscarf-values, include = FALSE}
headscarf_edges <- hg_get(headscarf)
n_alone <- sum(headscarf_edges$size == 1L)
headscarf_parts <- hg_measures(headscarf, what = "components")
largest_part <- head(headscarf_parts, 1)
```

The selected judgment cites `r headscarf$n_nodes` decisions in
`r headscarf$n_hyperedges` blocks, including `r n_alone` singleton blocks.
The plot encloses the members of each block with at least two decisions
and uses colour for block size. It follows the representation used in
Figure 3 of Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r headscarf-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7}
plot(headscarf, color_by = "size", labels = FALSE,
     legend_title = "block size")
```

There are `r nrow(headscarf_parts)` connected components. The largest
contains `r largest_part$n_nodes` cited decisions in
`r largest_part$n_edges` blocks. Components indicate chains of shared
block membership. Singleton citations appear outside the multi-member
regions unless the cited decision also belongs to another displayed block.

## Growth

`hg_growth()` counts nodes, hyperedges, distinct member sets, and
memberships on a measurement grid. With `mode = "cumulative"`, each row
summarises all observations up to its time. Inspecting all four counts
distinguishes growth in observations from growth in distinct combinations.

```{r gfcc-growth}
blocks_growth <- hg_growth(blocks, mode = "cumulative")
tail(blocks_growth, 3)
```

Plot the cumulative counts against calendar time, following the
quantities in Figure 4a of Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r gfcc-growth-plot}
plot(blocks_growth,
     columns = c("n_nodes", "n_edges", "n_edges_distinct", "n_memberships"))
```

The curves describe the accumulation of decisions, blocks, and
memberships. At the final time, there are
`r comma(tail(blocks_growth, 1)$n_edges)` blocks and
`r comma(tail(blocks_growth, 1)$n_edges_distinct)` distinct member sets.
Distinct sets account for
`r pct(tail(blocks_growth, 1)$n_edges_distinct / tail(blocks_growth, 1)$n_edges)`
of the block count. The visual trend should not be treated as a fitted
growth law without a separate model.

Block size is the number of distinct decisions cited in a block.
Compute its distribution for cumulative snapshots at the five specified
dates. Each snapshot contains all blocks observed up to its date.

```{r gfcc-sizes}
census_dates <- as.Date(c("1960-12-31", "1975-12-31", "1990-12-31",
                          "2005-12-31", "2020-12-31"))
block_sizes <- hg_edges(blocks, what = "distribution", measure = "size",
                        at = census_dates, snapshot_mode = "cumulative")
```

The complementary cumulative distribution gives the proportion of
blocks with size at least each value on the horizontal axis. This is the
quantity displayed in Figure 4b of Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r gfcc-sizes-plot}
plot(block_sizes)
```

```{r gfcc-sizes-values, include = FALSE}
size_summary <- hg_edges(blocks, what = "summary", measure = "size",
                         at = census_dates, snapshot_mode = "cumulative")
```

Across these snapshots, the largest observed block size ranges from
`r min(size_summary$max)` to `r max(size_summary$max)` decisions, and the
mean ranges from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(size_summary$mean))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(size_summary$mean))`. Read individual curves to
assess where in the distribution the temporal differences occur.

## Arbitrators and tribunals over time

For arbitrators, hyperdegree counts tribunal memberships. The
cumulative snapshot includes every tribunal observed by the selected date.

```{r icsid-degrees}
hg_get(tribunals_all, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree", top = 5)
tribunal_counts <- hg_measures(tribunals_all, what = "distribution",
                               measure = "hyperdegree")
```

```{r icsid-degrees-values, include = FALSE}
share_two <- 1 - subset(tribunal_counts, value == 3)$ccdf
top_arbitrators <- hg_get(tribunals_all, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree",
                          top = 2)
first_arbitrator <- head(top_arbitrators, 1)
second_arbitrator <- tail(top_arbitrators, 1)
```

The complementary cumulative plot summarises the distribution of
tribunal counts per arbitrator, corresponding to Figure 5a of Coupette
et al. (2024).

```{r icsid-degrees-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(tribunal_counts)
```

The observed distribution is highly unequal:
`r pct(share_two)` of arbitrators appear on one or two tribunals, while
`r first_arbitrator$node` appears on `r first_arbitrator$degree` and
`r second_arbitrator$node` on `r second_arbitrator$degree`. A long upper
tail in this plot is descriptive evidence of concentration; it does not
establish a particular heavy-tailed probability model.

For interval observations, the default growth view counts active
tribunals and their arbitrators. Columns ending in `_cumulative` retain
the counts of everything observed by that time. With `components = TRUE`,
the result also gives connected-component count, the proportion of active
nodes in the largest component, and its diameter.

```{r icsid-growth}
tribunals_growth <- hg_growth(tribunals, components = TRUE)
tail(tribunals_growth, 3)
```

```{r icsid-growth-values, include = FALSE}
last_growth <- tail(tribunals_growth, 1)
recent <- subset(tribunals_growth,
                 time >= as.numeric(as.Date("2007-01-01") - as.Date("1974-10-07")))
```

The plot compares active and cumulative counts, following Figure 5b
of Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r icsid-growth-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(tribunals_growth,
     columns = c("n_nodes", "n_edges", "n_nodes_cumulative",
                 "n_edges_cumulative"),
     facets = FALSE)
```

At the observation endpoint, `r last_growth$n_edges` of the
`r last_growth$n_edges_cumulative` tribunals are active, involving
`r last_growth$n_nodes` of the `r last_growth$n_nodes_cumulative`
arbitrators observed cumulatively. On the inspected grid since 2007, the
largest component contains between
`r pct(min(recent$largest_component))` and
`r pct(max(recent$largest_component))` of active arbitrators, with diameter
between `r min(recent$diameter)` and `r max(recent$diameter)`.
These values describe concurrent structure under the recorded intervals.

The external neighbourhood of a tribunal contains arbitrators outside
that tribunal who share another tribunal with at least one of its members.
`what = "summary"` reports the distribution of neighbourhood sizes across
active tribunals at each measurement time.

```{r icsid-neighbourhood}
neighbourhood <- hg_edges(tribunals, what = "summary", measure = "n_neighbors")
```

Plot the mean and quartiles to examine changes in tribunal
neighbourhood size, following Figure 5c of Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r icsid-neighbourhood-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(neighbourhood, columns = c("mean", "q25", "median", "q75"),
     facets = FALSE)
```

```{r icsid-neighbourhood-values, include = FALSE}
last_neighbourhood <- tail(neighbourhood, 1)
```

The final snapshot has median neighbourhood size
`r last_neighbourhood$median`. Comparing its mean, median, and quartiles
describes location and spread. Similar mean and median values alone are
insufficient to establish that the distribution is symmetric.

## Repeated collaboration

Define repeated-pair count as the total number of pair occurrences
across tribunals minus the number of distinct pairs. Repeated-edge count
is the number of tribunals minus the number of distinct three-arbitrator
panels. These statistics count additional occurrences, not just the
number of pairs or panels that recur.

The assignment null of Coupette et al. (2024) processes arbitrators in
decreasing hyperdegree and assigns each to available tribunal seats.
Successful draws preserve each arbitrator's tribunal count and each
tribunal's size. They are not uniform draws from all incidence matrices
with these margins. The following test uses 999 draws and compares the
observed repetition counts with this specified reference distribution.

```{r icsid-repeats}
repeats <- hg_null_test(tribunals_all,
                        statistic = c("repeated_pairs", "repeated_edges"),
                        method = "assignment", n = 999, seed = 1)
repeats
```

```{r icsid-repeats-values, include = FALSE}
repeat_row <- function(s, col) unlist(subset(repeats, statistic == s, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

The observed additional pair count is
`r repeat_row("repeated_pairs", "observed")`, compared with a central
95% null interval from `r repeat_row("repeated_pairs", "null_lo")` to
`r repeat_row("repeated_pairs", "null_hi")`. The corresponding panel
count is `r repeat_row("repeated_edges", "observed")`, with null interval
`r repeat_row("repeated_edges", "null_lo")` to
`r repeat_row("repeated_edges", "null_hi")`.
The table supplies the Monte Carlo p-values for the selected test.
An excess indicates repetition beyond this assignment model; it does
not identify the institutional or behavioural causes of the repetition.

## Hyperedge centrality

An s-line graph represents each hyperedge as a vertex and connects
two vertices when their hyperedges share at least s members. Hyperedge
s-betweenness counts shortest paths passing through a hyperedge, with
fractional contributions when several shortest paths exist. Hyperedge
s-closeness uses graph distances, with the Wasserman–Faust correction
for disconnected line graphs when normalisation is enabled.

At s = 1, two tribunals are adjacent when they share an arbitrator.
The following analysis uses tribunals active at the observation endpoint
and the normalisation convention used by NetworkX in the source study.

```{r icsid-betweenness}
central_cases <- hg_edge_centrality(tribunals_active, s = 1,
                                    measure = "betweenness", top = 10)
central_cases
```

```{r icsid-closeness}
hg_edge_centrality(tribunals_active, s = 1, measure = "closeness", top = 10)
```

```{r icsid-centrality-values, include = FALSE}
close_cases <- hg_edge_centrality(tribunals_active, s = 1,
                                  measure = "closeness", top = 10)
n_shared <- length(intersect(central_cases$edge, close_cases$edge))
```

Of the ten tribunals highest in betweenness, `r n_shared` also appear
among the ten highest in closeness. Select the ten highest-betweenness
tribunals with `hg_subset(edges = ...)` and colour them by economic sector.
This follows the display in Figure 6a of Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r icsid-central}
central_tribunals <- hg_subset(tribunals_active, edges = central_cases)
```

```{r icsid-central-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
plot(central_tribunals, color_by = "economic_sector",
     legend_title = "economic sector", label_size = 2.8)
```

```{r icsid-central-values, include = FALSE}
central_hub <- hg_get(central_tribunals, what = "nodes", sort_by = "degree",
                      top = 1)
```

Within this selected set, `r central_hub$node` appears on
`r central_hub$degree` tribunals, which collectively cover
`r length(unique(hg_get(central_tribunals, what = "edge_data")$economic_sector))`
economic sectors. Centrality describes connectivity through shared
arbitrators; the displayed sectors are attributes rather than inputs to
the centrality calculation.

## Motifs

For a simple three-uniform hypergraph, an induced set of four nodes
can contain up to four distinct three-node hyperedges. The labels Y, T,
and O denote configurations with exactly two, three, and four of these
hyperedges. The census first collapses repeated identical tribunals.

The configuration randomisation exchanges members between hyperedge pairs.
It preserves degrees and edge sizes before duplicate-edge collapse;
collapse can change the degrees in the simple hypergraphs used for the
census. The following comparison uses 300 draws on the aggregate of all
tribunals. It therefore uses a different null model from the assignment
test in the preceding section.

```{r icsid-motifs}
motifs <- hg_motifs(tribunals_all, n = 300, seed = 1)
motifs
```

```{r icsid-motifs-values, include = FALSE}
motif_row <- function(m, col) unlist(subset(motifs, motif == m, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

The plot compares the observed Y count with its simulated null
distribution, following the quantity displayed in Figure 7c of Coupette
et al. (2024).

```{r icsid-motifs-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(motifs)
```

The observed Y count is `r motif_row("Y", "count")`, with null mean
`r round(motif_row("Y", "expected"))` and standardised deviation
`r sprintf("%.1f", motif_row("Y", "z"))`. The T count is
`r motif_row("T", "count")`, with null mean
`r sprintf("%.1f", motif_row("T", "expected"))`.
An excess of Y indicates a concentration of induced four-arbitrator sets
containing two tribunals that share a pair. This is related to repeated
pair membership, but the motif census and repeated-pair test use
different counting rules and reference distributions.

## Communities of arbitrators

Hypergraph modularity assesses a node partition relative to a
degree-based reference model (Kamiński et al. 2019). For an edge e, let
its size be d_e and its weight be w_e. Let c_e be the largest number of
its members assigned to one community. Only an edge with a strict
majority in a community contributes to that community. Under the default
linear rule, its contribution is w_e times c_e/d_e.

The reference contribution, called `degree_tax` in the output, depends
on community degree shares. In the formula below, W_d is the total weight
of size-d hyperedges, p_A is the proportion of total weighted degree
held by community A, and omega(d,c) is c/d for c greater than d/2.

\[
T_A = \sum_d W_d \sum_{c > d/2} \omega(d, c)\,
\binom{d}{c} p_A^{\,c} (1 - p_A)^{d-c},
\]

The binomial term gives the reference probability of c of d positions
belonging to community A at degree share p_A. Let W be total hyperedge
weight and E_A the observed weighted majority contribution to A.
Modularity is the observed contribution minus this reference contribution,
divided by W:

\[
Q = \frac{1}{W}\Big(\sum_A E_A - \sum_A T_A\Big),
\qquad E_A = \sum_{e \text{ owned by } A} w_e\,\omega(d_e, c_e).
\]

A single-community partition has modularity zero under this
definition. Iteratively reweighted modularity maximisation (IRMM; Kumar
et al. 2020) alternates a weighted clique projection, Louvain graph
partitioning, and updates to hyperedge weights. It does not guarantee
the global optimum of the reported hypergraph modularity.

Use 20 seeds to examine optimisation variation. The reported medoid is
the run with the greatest summed adjusted mutual information with the
other runs. Graph modularity has a known resolution limit (Fortunato and
Barthélemy 2007), so inspect the sizes and stability of the resulting
communities rather than treating one partition as uniquely determined.

```{r icsid-irmm}
irmm <- hg_communities(tribunals_all, type = "irmm", seeds = 1:20,
                       n_runs = 20, max_iter = 300)
irmm
```

```{r icsid-irmm-values, include = FALSE}
irmm_sizes <- hg_get(irmm, what = "sizes")
irmm_runs <- hg_get(irmm, what = "runs")
irmm_ami <- hg_get(irmm, what = "ami")
```

The medoid contains `r nrow(irmm_sizes)` communities, with sizes from
`r min(irmm_sizes$n_nodes)` to `r max(irmm_sizes$n_nodes)` arbitrators.
The runs produce between `r min(irmm_runs$n_communities)` and
`r max(irmm_runs$n_communities)` communities. Median pairwise adjusted
mutual information is `r sprintf("%.2f", median(irmm_ami$ami))`.
Inspect the runs table for convergence before interpreting the medoid.
The next calculation scores that partition on the original hypergraph.

```{r icsid-modularity}
irmm_modularity <- hg_modularity(tribunals_all, irmm)
irmm_modularity
```

The medoid's normalised observed edge contribution is
`r sprintf("%.2f", irmm_modularity$edge_contribution)`, and its reference
contribution is `r sprintf("%.2f", irmm_modularity$degree_tax)`.
Their difference is the modularity,
`r sprintf("%.3f", irmm_modularity$modularity)`.
Across runs, modularity ranges from
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(irmm_runs$modularity))` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(irmm_runs$modularity))`. The per-community table
decomposes the total score.

```{r icsid-modularity-communities}
hg_modularity(tribunals_all, irmm, what = "communities")
```

```{r icsid-modularity-communities-values, include = FALSE}
by_community <- hg_modularity(tribunals_all, irmm, what = "communities")
small <- subset(by_community, n_nodes == 3L)
```

Inspect community contributions alongside their sizes and volumes.
The `r nrow(small)` communities containing three arbitrators include
small groups that should be checked against the component structure.
Community size alone does not establish that a group is an isolated
tribunal or that its members have no other appointments.

The following plot shows the previously selected central tribunals,
with each arbitrator's colour and shape indicating its IRMM community.

```{r icsid-communities-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
plot(central_tribunals, node_groups = irmm, label_size = 2.8)
```

```{r icsid-communities-plot-values, include = FALSE}
central_partition <- merge(hg_get(central_tribunals, what = "memberships"),
                           hg_get(irmm), by = "node")
n_central_communities <- length(unique(central_partition$community))
n_central_arbitrators <- length(unique(central_partition$node))
communities_per_case <- aggregate(community ~ hyperedge, data = central_partition,
                                  FUN = \(x) length(unique(x)))
n_mixed <- sum(communities_per_case$community > 1L)
```

The `r n_central_arbitrators` displayed arbitrators belong to
`r n_central_communities` communities. Of the ten tribunals,
`r n_mixed` include members from more than one community.
This compares a line-graph centrality ranking with a node partition;
the two analyses describe different structural features.

Infomap minimises the description length of a random walk on a graph
(Rosvall and Bergstrom 2008). The default `hg_communities()` applies it
to the association projection, where a hyperedge of size d adds
1/(d−1) to each pairwise edge among its members. This differs from
ordinary shared-hyperedge counts when hyperedge sizes vary.

```{r icsid-infomap}
infomap <- hg_communities(tribunals_all, seeds = 1:20, n_runs = 20)
hg_modularity(tribunals_all, infomap)
```

```{r icsid-infomap-values, include = FALSE}
infomap_sizes <- hg_get(infomap, what = "sizes")
infomap_modularity <- hg_modularity(tribunals_all, infomap)
infomap_ami <- hg_get(infomap, what = "ami")
```

The Infomap medoid has `r nrow(infomap_sizes)` communities, with
largest size `r max(infomap_sizes$n_nodes)`. Its observed edge
contribution is `r sprintf("%.2f", infomap_modularity$edge_contribution)`,
reference contribution is `r sprintf("%.2f", infomap_modularity$degree_tax)`,
and hypergraph modularity is
`r sprintf("%.3f", infomap_modularity$modularity)`.
Median agreement across Infomap runs is
`r sprintf("%.2f", median(infomap_ami$ami))`. Compare the medoids
directly to assess how much the two objectives change the partition.

```{r icsid-agreement}
hg_agreement(irmm, infomap, method = c("ari", "ami"))
```

```{r icsid-agreement-values, include = FALSE}
partition_agreement <- hg_agreement(irmm, infomap, method = c("ari", "ami"))
```

The medoids agree with adjusted Rand index
`r sprintf("%.2f", partition_agreement$ari)` and adjusted mutual
information `r sprintf("%.2f", partition_agreement$ami)`.
The largest Infomap community contains
`r max(infomap_sizes$n_nodes)` arbitrators, compared with
`r max(irmm_sizes$n_nodes)` for IRMM. These differences are outcomes of
the specified objectives, projections, and optimisation settings; they
do not identify a single objectively correct division of the arbitrators.

## Communities of decisions across representations

The GFCC comparison follows eight representations used by Coupette
et al. (2024). Citation graphs differ by edge multiplicity and direction.
Association projections differ by repeated-hyperedge handling and by
self-association, which adds links from a citing decision to the cited
members of its blocks. The analysis retains backward citations, for which
the cited decision predates the citing decision. The next specification
table makes the abbreviated representation labels explicit.

| Label | Projection | Repeated observations | Direction | Self-association |
|:------|:-----------|:----------------------|:----------|:-----------------|
| `bg` | Citation | Collapsed | Directed | Not applicable |
| `bgu` | Citation | Collapsed | Undirected | Not applicable |
| `mg` | Citation | Counted | Directed | Not applicable |
| `mgu` | Citation | Counted | Undirected | Not applicable |
| `bh` | Association | Collapsed | Undirected | Excluded |
| `bhs` | Association | Collapsed | Undirected | Included |
| `mh` | Association | Counted | Undirected | Excluded |
| `mhs` | Association | Counted | Undirected | Included |

```{r gfcc-backward}
backward_citations <- subset(gfcc_citations, date_citing > date_cited)
backward <- temporal_hypergraph(backward_citations, node = "cited",
                                hyperedge = "block", time = "date_citing",
                                nodes = gfcc_decisions, sparse = TRUE)
backward_all <- hg_snapshot(backward, mode = "cumulative")
```

Each representation is fitted with five seeds and five Infomap
trials per seed. The source study uses 50 seeds and 100 trials, so this
tutorial explores a smaller optimisation ensemble. Use
`method = "citation"` for citation graphs,
`duplicate_edges = "collapse"` for collapsed repeated observations,
and `self_association = TRUE` to include the citing-decision term.

```{r gfcc-communities-graphs, eval = has_igraph}
communities_bg <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                 seeds = 1:5, method = "citation",
                                 edge_source = "citing",
                                 duplicate_edges = "collapse", directed = TRUE)
communities_bgu <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                  seeds = 1:5, method = "citation",
                                  edge_source = "citing",
                                  duplicate_edges = "collapse")
communities_mg <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                 seeds = 1:5, method = "citation",
                                 edge_source = "citing", directed = TRUE)
communities_mgu <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                  seeds = 1:5, method = "citation",
                                  edge_source = "citing")
```

```{r gfcc-communities-hypergraphs, eval = has_igraph}
communities_bh <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                 seeds = 1:5, duplicate_edges = "collapse")
communities_bhs <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                  seeds = 1:5, duplicate_edges = "collapse",
                                  self_association = TRUE,
                                  edge_source = "citing")
communities_mh <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                 seeds = 1:5)
communities_mhs <- hg_communities(backward_all, n_runs = 5, trials = 5,
                                  seeds = 1:5, self_association = TRUE,
                                  edge_source = "citing")
```

`hg_compare_communities()` reports partition sizes and agreement.
When `hg` is supplied, it also calculates quality measures on each fit's
saved projection. These quality measures are defined here for undirected
graphs. The two directed citation fits therefore receive missing quality
scores and an explanatory warning.

```{r gfcc-compare, eval = has_igraph}
comparison <- hg_compare_communities(
  bg = communities_bg, bgu = communities_bgu, mg = communities_mg,
  mgu = communities_mgu, bh = communities_bh, bhs = communities_bhs,
  mh = communities_mh, mhs = communities_mhs,
  hg = backward_all
)
comparison
```

```{r gfcc-compare-values, eval = has_igraph, include = FALSE}
compare_summary <- hg_get(comparison)
model_row <- function(m, col) unlist(subset(compare_summary, model == m, select = col), use.names = FALSE)
```

Without self-association, the medoids contain
`r comma(model_row("bh", "n_singletons"))` (`bh`) and
`r comma(model_row("mh", "n_singletons"))` (`mh`) singleton communities.
Uncited decisions have no membership connections in these association
graphs. Adding self-association gives
`r comma(model_row("bhs", "n_singletons"))` singletons for `bhs`, compared
with `r comma(model_row("bg", "n_singletons"))` in the binary citation
graph. Singleton communities need not all be isolated vertices, so inspect
the graph when attributing their origin. The plot follows Figure 8b of
Coupette et al. (2024).

```{r gfcc-compare-plot, eval = has_igraph, fig.height = 4}
plot(comparison)
```

The community-size distributions differ particularly at the smallest
and largest sizes. Largest-community sizes are
`r model_row("bg", "largest_size")` for `bg`,
`r model_row("bgu", "largest_size")` for `bgu`, and
`r model_row("mh", "largest_size")` for `mh`. Use adjusted mutual
information and the adjusted Rand index to compare membership directly;
similar size distributions alone do not imply similar partitions.

```{r gfcc-similarity, eval = has_igraph, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
plot(comparison, what = "similarity")
```

```{r gfcc-similarity-values, eval = has_igraph, include = FALSE}
similarity <- hg_get(comparison, what = "similarity")
hyper <- c("bh", "bhs", "mh", "mhs")
within_hyper <- subset(similarity, model_a %in% hyper & model_b %in% hyper)
across <- subset(similarity, xor(model_a %in% hyper, model_b %in% hyper))
```

The matrix displays adjusted mutual information below the diagonal
and the adjusted Rand index above it, following Figure 8c of Coupette
et al. (2024). Mean adjusted mutual information is
`r sprintf("%.2f", mean(within_hyper$ami))` within the four association
representations and `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(across$ami))` between an
association and a citation representation. The subsequent table reports
coverage, performance, modularity, and worst-community conductance for
the eligible undirected fits.

```{r gfcc-quality, eval = has_igraph}
hg_get(comparison, what = "quality")
```

```{r gfcc-quality-values, eval = has_igraph, include = FALSE}
quality <- hg_get(comparison, what = "quality")
quality_hyper <- subset(quality, model %in% hyper)
quality_graph <- subset(quality, !model %in% hyper & !is.na(modularity))
```

Graph modularity ranges from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(quality_hyper$modularity))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(quality_hyper$modularity))` across association
representations, and from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(quality_graph$modularity))` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(quality_graph$modularity))` across undirected
citation representations. Each score uses a different graph and reference
distribution. These values describe partition structure within each
representation and do not rank the partitions on a common objective.

## Interpretation

The tutorial shows how the observation unit and temporal rule change
the quantities reported for the same entities. Arbitrator hyperdegree
counts tribunal participation, graph degree counts distinct colleagues,
and repetition statistics retain information about observed panels.
For citation data, block membership and source-to-target citation edges
also define different relations.

Centrality, motifs, and community detection address separate structural
questions. Their results depend on the snapshot, projection, null model,
and optimisation objective. They should be interpreted as analyses of
recorded relationships, with substantive explanations requiring additional
institutional evidence.

## Limitations

Observation ends on 15 June 2023. Pending cases are right-censored,
and the recorded case interval is an approximation to the time during
which tribunal membership is relevant. The assignment null preserves
margins but does not sample uniformly over all matching hypergraphs.
The motif randomisation also includes duplicate collapse, which changes
the final simple-hypergraph degree sequences.

The tutorial uses 300 motif draws and five GFCC seeds with five trials,
compared with 1,000 draws and 50 seeds with 100 trials in the source study.
Smaller ensembles give less precise tail estimates and a more limited
assessment of optimisation variability. Majority-based hypergraph
modularity counts a three-member tribunal split two-to-one as contributing
to the majority community. This convention should accompany its reported
score. None of these structural measures establishes the legal importance
of a case or a causal mechanism of appointment.
